idiom_name: sealed trait + final case class nodes with named fields
implementation_notes: Case classes are the canonical Scala AST node: a sealed trait plus final case class Binary(left: Expr, op: String, right: Expr) declares the named children as constructor parameters and synthesises structural equality, copy and extractors, while match implements node-specific traversal with exhaustivity diagnostics. This is how scala.reflect trees and most Scala compilers represent syntax; the classic visitor is replaced by one match function per operation.
code_sketch:
sealed trait Expr
final case class Lit(value: Int) extends Expr
final case class Binary(left: Expr, op: String, right: Expr) extends Expr   // named children

def print(e: Expr): String = e match {
  case Lit(v)          => v.toString
  case Binary(l, o, r) => s"(${print(l)} $o ${print(r)})"
}
pitfalls: Exhaustivity is a warning, not an error (E029): a missing case fails at run time with MatchError unless the build escalates the warning.
Case-class equality, hashCode and copy recurse through the whole tree, so deep structural comparisons and case-class rewrites are expensive; use identity (eq) when that is what is meant.

variants.name: Scala 3 enum with parameterised cases
variants.implementation_notes: Scala 3's enum declaration expresses the same nodes with parameterised cases (case Binary(left: Expr, op: String, right: Expr)), which the compiler expands to a sealed class hierarchy whose fields are the named children; matching and exhaustivity behave as for case classes with less boilerplate and one declaration. Choose it on Scala 3 codebases, and keep the sealed-trait encoding when nodes must extend other traits or the library still cross-compiles to Scala 2.13.
variants.code_sketch:
enum Expr:
  case Lit(value: Int)
  case Binary(left: Expr, op: String, right: Expr)   // named parameters per case

def print(e: Expr): String = e match
  case Expr.Lit(v)          => v.toString
  case Expr.Binary(l, o, r) => s"(${print(l)} $o ${print(r)})"
pitfalls: Enum cases cannot reference inner members or companion members by simple name (a documented restriction), which surprises code migrated from sealed traits.
Cross-compiling to Scala 2 forces the sealed-trait encoding, so mixed-version libraries end up maintaining both forms.
